newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerians get elections but no constitution yet.
newsitem.headline: Nigerians get elections but no constitution yet.

text.p: Nigeria's military government has cited enthusiastic voting in local elections as proof of popular support for its disputed civil-rule plan.
But political analysts cautioned that the future of democracy in the West African nation was far from clear with no sign of a constitution to serve as a blueprint for a new order.
Military ruler General Sani Abacha, urged by supporters to prolong his rule as a civilian president, has yet to promulgate a draft constitution completed over a year ago.
No one outside Abacha's small circle of confidants knows when the constitution will be promulgated, even though by his own promise, constitutional rule must start by October 1, 1998.

"What I do not seem to understand is whether there is indeed any constitutional or plain legal principles applicable to the present transition exercise," wrote columnist Mike Ikhariale on Tuesday in the National Concord, a newspaper owned by jailed presidential claimant Moshood Abiola.
A legal expert serving on one of Abacha's numerous transition committees said privately that holding elections in a constitutional void amounted to a meaningless exercise.
"Without a constitution offices are not defined so people don't really know what they are running for," said the expert who asked not to be named.

"There are too many unanswered questions -- will the president be elected on the basis of national suffrage? Will a group of parties be allowed to agree on one common candidate for president as some are trying to do?," he asked.
Abacha seized power in 1993 after previous army rulers aborted a plan to return Nigeria to civil rule, sparking unrest.
He ignored pressure at home and from the West for an early return to democracy and pressed on with his own civil-rule plan. Saturday's poll was the first on party lines since 1993.
A constitution drafting committee submitted its work in June 1995 and he promised a national charter would be ready later last year after approval by the military's ruling council.
In a recent interview with the Washington Times Abacha said it was for a civilian government to promulgate the constitution.
Two of the five political parties registered by the military have stated officially that they want to draft Abacha to run for president next year as a "consensus" candidate.
The fact that results of the weekend local elections have shown the two headed for supremacy nationwide has fuelled speculation that they were sponsored by the government as a platform for Abacha.

Abacha's only comment about his possible candidacy is that it depends on his "constituency." He has not stated if the constituency is the army or another group but supporters say he is as free as anyone to run once he quits the army.

In nationwide tallies from provincial electoral authorities published in newspapers, the United Nigeria Congress Party spearheading the "draft-Abacha" campaign swept to victory in 251 of 531 local councils declared from a national total of 774.
The Democratic Party of Nigeria which also favours Abacha as a common candidate took 150 councils with the three other parties sharing the rest of the declared town halls.
The Congress Party even won comfortably in stronghold states of presidential claimant Abiola, who has been in detention since declaring himself head of state in 1994 after the annulled elections.
"I think most Nigerians have concluded that there is no point standing in front of a moving train," said an Abiola supporter in Lagos, where opposition to Abacha is strong.
Nigerian political activist Yima Sen said the results reflected the continuing power of government patronage, especially at a time of severe economic hardship.

"People have benefited from the system. The system has mobilised. It is expected that people will go back to the grassroots and mobilise support for parties seen as government sponsored," Sen told Reuters.

But he said he expected the politcal landscape to change dramatically when many experienced and influential politicians whose parties were not registered joined the fray in forthcoming state and national elections. Most ignored the local polls.
Authorities in the country's 36 states invariably declared voter turnout as "impressive" but none gave precise figures.
Judged by a history of polling day thuggery, bloodshed and chaos, the orderly polling on Saturday stunned even avowed enemies of the military government.
At least three people were reported killed in scattered poll violence and police made scores of arrests but none of that compares with turbulent elections in the past.
